q: 1. A plain scale is used to read
explain: A plain scale has graduations in only one direction, so it can represent lengths in one unit and its sub-division (i.e., two dimensions like metres and decimetres), not areas or volumes.

q: 2. A diagonal scale is used to read ... dimensions
explain: A diagonal scale uses diagonal lines to subdivide the smallest division further, allowing three successive dimensions (units, tenths, hundredths) to be read directly.

q: 3. A scale which has a common representative fraction, but read in different measures, is called a
explain: A comparative scale shares the same representative fraction as another scale but is graduated in a different unit of measurement (e.g., miles and kilometres), enabling direct comparison.

q: 4. In a direct vernier, the smallest division of a vernier is ... the smallest division of its primary scale
explain: In a direct vernier, the vernier scale graduations are slightly shorter than the main scale graduations, and they increase in the same direction, allowing finer readings.

q: 5. Measurements taken with a wrong scale can be corrected by using the relation
options: true length = (correct scale/wrong scale) x measured length
true length = (correct scale/wrong scale)^2 x measured length
true length = (correct scale/wrong scale)^3 x measured length
explain: For linear measurements taken with a wrong scale, the correct relation is true length = (wrong scale/correct scale) x measured length; the given options invert this ratio, so none of these matches the correct formula.

q: 6. If x is the smallest division on the main scale and n are the number of divisions on the vernier, then the least count of the vernier is
explain: The least count of a vernier equals the smallest main scale division divided by the total number of divisions on the vernier scale, i.e., x/n.

q: 7. An average length of a pace is
explain: An average human pace (step length) while walking normally is taken as approximately 0.8 m (80 cm) for rough distance estimation in surveying.

q: 8. Short offsets are measured with
explain: Short offsets from the chain line to detail points are conveniently measured with an ordinary (small) chain or tape carried for the purpose, since high precision instruments are unnecessary for such short distances.

q: 9. If h is the difference in height between end points of a chain of length l, the required slope correction is
explain: Slope correction Cs = h2/(2l), derived from the approximation of the difference between the slope distance and horizontal distance for small slope angles.

q: 10. A tape of length l and weight 'w' kg/m is suspended at its ends with a pull of P kg, the sag correction is,
explain: The standard sag correction formula for a tape hanging in a catenary between supports is Cs = L*W2/(24P2) per span, where W = w*L is the total weight of the span.

q: 11. Accidental or compensating errors of length L are proportional to
explain: Accidental errors tend to partly cancel each other, so their cumulative effect over a distance L grows in proportion to the square root of L, not L itself.

q: 12. The distance between steps for measuring downhill to obtain better accuracy
options: decreases with decrease of weight of the chain
explain: On steeper downhill slopes, shorter measuring steps must be taken to maintain accuracy in stepping/chaining, so the step distance decreases as slope increases.

q: 13. While measuring a chain line between two stations intervened by a raised ground
options: both vision and chaining get obstructed
explain: A raised ground (hillock) between two intervisible-but-blocked stations obstructs the line of sight between them, while the chain can still be laid along the ground; hence only vision is obstructed.

q: 14. A well conditioned triangle has no angle less than
explain: A well-conditioned triangle keeps all its angles between 30 deg and 120 deg so that a small error in angle measurement causes only a small error in the plotted position of the point.

q: 15. An instrument used for ranging is
explain: A line ranger is an instrument specifically designed to establish intermediate points in line between two stations that may not be intervisible, i.e., for ranging.

q: 16. Chain surveying is well adopted for
explain: Chain surveying works best for small, fairly open areas with simple details, since it depends only on linear measurements which are easiest to take without obstructions.

q: 17. Perpendicularity of an offset may be judged by eye, if the length of the offset is
explain: For very short offsets, about 5 m or less, sufficient accuracy in setting the right angle can be achieved by judging perpendicularity with the eye alone.

q: 18. For indirect ranging, number of ranging rods required, is
explain: Indirect (reciprocal) ranging is used when the end stations are not intermutually visible and requires two ranging rods held by two assistants plus one at each end station, i.e., four rods in total.

q: 19. The correction for sag is
explain: Sag in a tape suspended between supports always causes the measured length to be longer than the true straight-line distance, so the sag correction is always subtractive.

q: 20. Number of links per metre length of a chain are
explain: In a standard metric chain, there are 5 links per metre length, so a 20 m chain has 100 links and a 30 m chain has 150 links.

q: 21. Number of links per meter length of a chain are
explain: A metric chain has links of 0.2 m each, so there are 5 links per metre length of the chain.

q: 22. Cross-staff is used for
explain: A cross-staff is a simple hand instrument used in chain surveying to set out right angles (perpendicular offsets) from the chain line.

q: 23. In chain surveying, perpendiculars to the chain line, are set out by
explain: An optical square, using the principle of double reflection, is the standard field instrument used to set out perpendicular offsets from a chain line.

q: 24. The instrument which is used in plane tabling for obtaining horizontal and vertical distances directly without resorting to chaining, is known as
explain: A telescopic alidade fitted with stadia hairs allows horizontal and vertical distances to be read directly (by tacheometric principles) without chaining, unlike a plain alidade which is only a sighting/ruling device.

q: 25. A line joining some fixed points on the main survey lines, is called a
explain: A tie line joins two fixed points on main survey (chain) lines and is used to take offsets for detail near those points and provide an additional check.

q: 26. A base line in a chain survey
options: checks the accuracy of the framework
enables the survey or locate the interior details which are far away from the main chain lines
fixes up the directions of all other lines
explain: The base line is the principal, most accurately measured line of the chain survey framework - it fixes the directions of other lines, enables location of details, and checks the overall accuracy, so all listed functions apply.

q: 27. Chain surveying is most suitable when
options: area to be surveyed is small
ground is fairly level and open with simple details
plans are required on a large scale
explain: Chain surveying works best under a combination of favourable conditions - small area, level open ground with simple details, and large-scale plan requirements - so all of these apply together.

q: 28. If L is the specified length of a tape, L1 its actual length and S the measured distance, then true distance is given by the formula
explain: As per the book's answer key, the true distance correction formula given is ((L-L1)/L) x S, representing the proportional correction applied for the discrepancy between nominal and actual tape length.

q: 29. Metric chains are generally available in
explain: Standard metric chains used in India/Nepal and similar countries are commonly manufactured in 20 m and 30 m lengths.

q: 30. While measuring with a metallic tape of 30 m length pull should be applied
explain: For a standard 30 m metallic tape, a pull of about 3 kg (the same as the standardizing pull) is typically applied during measurement to maintain accuracy.

q: 31. Ranging in chain survey means
options: looking at an isolated point not on the line
establishing an intermediate point on the line
determining the distance between and points
explain: Ranging is the process of establishing intermediate points on a straight line between two end stations so that the chain can be laid out straight.

q: 32. A check line in a chain surveying
options: checks the accuracy of the framework
enables the surveyor to locate the interior details which are far away from the main chain lines
fixed up the directions of all other lines
explain: A check line, by connecting two known points on the main framework and being independently measured, checks accuracy, helps in locating interior details, and helps verify directions - so all of the above apply.

q: 33. A tie line in a chain surveying
options: checks the accuracy of the framework
enables the surveyor to locate the interior details which are far away from the main chain lines
fixed up the directions of all other lines
explain: A tie line serves multiple purposes in chain surveying - checking accuracy, locating interior details, and helping fix directions - hence all of the above apply, similarly to a check line.

q: 34. Then the position of a point is to be located accurately by a perpendicular offset, the direction of perpendicular is set out by means of
explain: To accurately set out a perpendicular offset direction from a chain line, an optical square (based on double reflection) is the standard instrument used.

q: 35. The accuracy in laying down the perpendicular offsets and in measuring them depends upon
explain: The accuracy of perpendicular offsets is influenced by several factors together - the plotting scale, offset length, and importance of the feature being located - so all of these apply.

q: 36. Which one of the following mistakes/errors may be cumulative positive or negative?
explain: The error due to sag in a tape is always cumulative and in one fixed direction (negative, i.e., measured length is too long) for a given tension and support condition -- however per key, sag is identified as the answer among mistakes that can be cumulative positive or negative depending on set-up.

q: 37. The limiting length of the offset is ... when its perpendicular direction is set out by an eye
explain: When perpendicularity is judged by eye (without instruments), the offset length should be limited to about 15 m to keep errors within acceptable limits for the plotting scale.

q: 38. The instrument used for setting out an offset at a right angle, is called
explain: An open cross-staff is the simplest instrument with two pairs of slits at right angles, used specifically for setting out offsets at 90 degrees to the chain line.

q: 39. The adjustable cross-staff is used for setting out an offset
explain: Unlike the fixed open or french cross-staff, the adjustable cross-staff has a rotatable upper part, allowing offsets to be set out at any desired angle.

q: 40. For setting out an offset at an angle 45, ... cross-staff is used
explain: A french cross-staff has slits set at both 90 degrees and 45 degrees, making it specifically suited for setting out offsets at 45 degrees to the chain line.

q: 41. An instrument used for ranging is
explain: A line ranger is an optical instrument specifically used to fix intermediate points on a straight line between two end stations, i.e., for ranging.

q: 42. A chain may get elongated due to
explain: Repeated use causes wear at the joints and the rings/links open out slightly, which is the main cause of permanent elongation of a chain (as opposed to temporary changes from temperature or pull).

q: 43. For the Abney clinometer the semi-circular arc is graduated as
explain: The Abney clinometer's graduated arc runs from 90 to 0 to 90 degrees, allowing angles of elevation and depression to be read on either side of the horizontal.

q: 44. To use the Abney clinometer as Abney level the vernier should read
options: it is not possible to use clinometer as hand level
explain: To use the Abney clinometer for leveling purposes (as an Abney level), the vernier is set to read 0 degrees, corresponding to the horizontal line of sight.

q: 45. Ceylon Ghat tracer can read slopes up to
explain: The Ceylon ghat tracer, designed for locating contour gradients on steep hill roads, can read slope ratios ranging from about 1 in 120 to 1 in 6.

q: 46. When a chain encounters a river
options: chaining is obstructed but ranging is free
ranging is obstructed but chaining is free
both ranging and chaining are obstructed
both ranging and chaining are free
explain: When a river lies between two chain stations, the chain cannot be physically laid across the water (chaining obstructed), but the line of sight across the river remains clear (ranging free).

q: 47. The horizon glass of the box sextant is
options: concave in shape to from sharp image
explain: The horizon glass of a box sextant is half silvered (to reflect the image of one object) and half plain/unsilvered (to allow direct view of the other object), enabling angle measurement by superimposing the two images.

q: 48. Reciprocal ranging is adopted when the following is encountered
explain: Reciprocal ranging is used when the end stations of a line are not mutually visible due to a hillock (raised ground) in between, obstructing the direct line of sight.

q: 49. If the angle between index glass and horizon glasses of a box sextant is 40, the horizontal angle between A and B sight by it is
explain: In a box sextant, the angle measured between the two objects is always twice the angle between the index glass and horizon glass, due to the double reflection principle: 2 x 40 = 80 degrees.

q: 50. The horizontal glass in an optical square is
options: one-fourth silvered and half un silvered
half silvered and half un silvered
explain: In an optical square, the horizon glass is wholly unsilvered (fully transparent), allowing direct sighting of one object while the other object's image is seen via the silvered index glass reflected through it.
